### Where AI struggled or failed

1. Context‑heavy decisions

On Day 3, I tried something ambitious: asking AI to help prioritize my weekly tasks.

I pasted my messy to‑do list:

Then I asked:

“Prioritize these tasks for maximum impact this week. Consider client deadlines, team expectations, and long‑term goals.”

The AI gave me a neat prioritized list… that was subtly wrong.

It put the analytics review near the top (important but not urgent), and the partner email near the bottom (urgent and relationship‑sensitive). It couldn’t see that this partner was currently frustrated, that the email had political weight, or that my manager cared a lot about it.

The AI was optimizing based on generic heuristics, not the messy reality of my job.

2. Nuanced interpersonal communication [...] ## Day 7: What Actually Changed in My Work

On the final day, I stopped trying to force AI into every corner and instead observed what had actually shifted in my work.

### Speed

Overall, I was faster at some things:

But I wasn’t dramatically faster at everything. Tasks that were already simple — a two‑line Slack message, a quick decision about a calendar slot — sometimes became slower if I tried to drag AI into them.

The net effect: my week felt more efficient, but not like I’d gained an extra four hours a day.

### Quality

The quality of my work was… different.

Where the quality improved the most was in things I’d normally rush: routine docs, status updates, simple FAQs. AI made those better with relatively little effort.

Surprisingly, my workday felt both less and more stressful.

If I had to sum it up: AI reduced the pain of starting, but increased the mental load of verifying.
